title: App Manual
summary: Use the app itself first: where to start, how daily study works, how to type Korean, and how to read the big picture before Chapter 1.

units.title: How to use this app
units.situation: You opened Korean Core Starter and want a simple daily route instead of wandering through every tab.
units.goal: I can choose what to do first, study for 15 minutes, and understand how review, romanization, and progress fit together.

beginnerGuide.title: The six tabs
beginnerGuide.body: Learn is the course path. Practice is review and drills. Shadow is speaking imitation. Roleplay is guided conversation. Dictionary is the reference. Guide is practical help for Korea and for using this app.

beginnerGuide.title: A 15-minute day
beginnerGuide.body: Start with Practice and clear due review for about 5 minutes. Open Learn for a few new screens for about 8 minutes. Finish with one Shadow line for about 2 minutes so the language reaches your mouth.

beginnerGuide.title: How review works
beginnerGuide.body: Items you miss can return through spaced review. The app brings them back after longer gaps so weak words stop disappearing.

beginnerGuide.title: Romanization
beginnerGuide.body: Keep Romaja on at the very beginning. Around Chapter 3, try turning it off for short stretches so Hangul starts doing the work.

beginnerGuide.title: Progress and backup
beginnerGuide.body: Completion is stored in this browser. When backup/export is added, use it before changing devices. Until then, keep the same browser for steady progress.

steps: Open Practice and clear anything due.
Open Learn and continue the next unfinished chapter or pack.
Add new words to review only when you want them to return later.
Use Dictionary when a word appears twice and still feels slippery.
Use Shadow or Roleplay briefly after study so the sentence becomes speakable.
Come back to Guide when a real-life Korea task blocks you.
checkpoints: I know what each tab is for.
I can follow the 15-minute daily route.
I know Romaja is temporary support, not the final reading habit.
I know progress lives in this browser unless I export it later.

units.title: Set up Korean typing
units.situation: You need to type Korean for drills, search, messages, delivery apps, maps, and daily life.
units.goal: I can install a Korean keyboard, switch to it, and use tap-input fallback when I do not have Korean typing ready.

beginnerGuide.title: Why this matters
beginnerGuide.body: Typing Korean lets you search Naver Map, text people, use delivery apps, and complete production drills. The app also gives tap-input fallback for typed answers so you are not blocked on day one.

beginnerGuide.title: iPhone or iPad
beginnerGuide.body: Open Settings > General > Keyboard > Keyboards > Add New Keyboard > Korean. Use the globe key to switch keyboards.

beginnerGuide.title: Android
beginnerGuide.body: In Gboard or Samsung Keyboard, open Languages, add Korean, and choose 2-set Korean. Use the globe or spacebar switcher to change languages.

beginnerGuide.title: Mac
beginnerGuide.body: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Input Sources, add Korean, and choose 2-Set Korean. Control-Space usually switches input sources.

beginnerGuide.title: Windows
beginnerGuide.body: Open Settings > Time & language > Language & region, add Korean, then switch with Win-Space. Choose the Korean Microsoft IME.

beginnerGuide.title: 2-set in 30 seconds
beginnerGuide.body: Consonants are on the left, vowels are on the right, and final consonants combine automatically. Type ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ and the keyboard builds 한.

steps: Install Korean input for your device.
Practice switching between English and Korean.
Type 한, 국, 어 slowly and watch the blocks combine.
Open Chapter 1 and use the Hangul trainer.
When a typing question appears before you are ready, use the tap-input fallback.
checkpoints: I can switch to Korean input.
I know 2-set Korean uses left-hand consonants and right-hand vowels.
I know the app has a tap-input fallback for typed drills.

units.title: How Korean Works
units.situation: A quick map of Korean before grammar details start.
units.goal: I can explain the ten big ideas that make the first chapters less surprising.

beginnerGuide.title: A five-minute map
beginnerGuide.body: These ten cards explain Hangul, word order, particles, politeness, dropped subjects, numbers, and sound changes before you meet them one by one in the course.

checkpoints: I know Korean verbs usually come at the end.
I know particles show noun roles.
I know Romaja is temporary support.
